title: Eventhouse and KQL Databases: The Real-Time Intelligence Engine in Microsoft Fabric
summary: A comprehensive practitioner reference covering Eventhouse architecture, KQL databases, OneLake integration, cost and capacity mechanics, security, and operational best practices — every claim grounded in verified Microsoft sources.
body_md:
## What Is an Eventhouse?

An Eventhouse is a workspace-level container in Microsoft Fabric's Real-Time Intelligence workload, designed to handle high-volume telemetry, event streams, and time-series data at any scale. It acts as an organizational envelope that can host multiple KQL (Kusto Query Language) databases, allowing them to share the underlying compute capacity rather than each provisioning their own isolated resources [S1].

The practical effect of that shared-capacity model is significant: you pay for one pool of Fabric Capacity Units and distribute that pool across all databases in the Eventhouse. Cost and performance optimization therefore happen jointly, at the container level, rather than in isolation per database [S1].

From a data-movement perspective, everything ingested into an Eventhouse is also automatically mirrored to OneLake as a single logical copy, making that data immediately reachable by every other Fabric experience — Lakehouse, Warehouse, Spark, Power BI — without any additional ETL [S2].

![Eventhouse and KQL database architecture](/content/diagrams/eventhouse-kql.svg)

## Core Concepts

### Automatic Time-Ordered Organization

Eventhouses automatically organize ingested records by arrival time. This time-ordering is the foundation of the fast, indexed queries that KQL databases deliver over structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data [S2]. Unlike a relational database where you explicitly design clustered keys, the Eventhouse engine arranges data as it lands, making range scans over timestamps extremely efficient by default.

### Dual Query Surface: KQL and T-SQL

Every Eventhouse database exposes data through two distinct query interfaces. The primary interface is native KQL — the pipe-based, columnar query language purpose-built for time-series and log analytics. The secondary interface is a T-SQL analytics endpoint, managed and governed within Fabric, that accepts standard SQL syntax [S2]. KQL querysets also support T-SQL access where applicable.

This dual-surface design matters for adoption: BI analysts and SQL developers can connect their existing tools without learning KQL, while data engineers and power users can exploit the full expressiveness of KQL's operators — `summarize`, `mv-expand`, `make-series`, and the native anomaly-detection functions [S2].

### OneLake as a Peer Consumer

OneLake availability can be turned on at the database level — covering all current and future tables with an option to backfill existing data — or at the individual table level for finer control [S1]. Once enabled, KQL table data is exposed in Delta Lake format, making it directly queryable by Power BI Direct Lake mode, Warehouse, Lakehouse, and Spark notebooks without any data movement or copy [S1]. There is no additional storage charge for the OneLake copy beyond the standard OneLake storage tier already billed [S1].

The KQL retention policy governs the OneLake copy in lockstep: when data ages out of the KQL database, it is concurrently soft-deleted from OneLake [S1]. This means you have one lifecycle policy, not two to maintain.

### Shortcuts into KQL Databases

A shortcut created inside a KQL database lands in the database's Shortcuts folder and is treated as an external table. To query it, you use the `external_table()` Kusto function rather than referencing it as a native table [S3]. This lets a KQL database reach data in OneLake, Azure Data Lake Storage, or other supported sources without copying data in.

## Architecture and Monitoring

### Container-Level Visibility

Monitoring is surfaced at two granularities. At the Eventhouse container level, a single system-overview page tracks storage consumption, compute utilization, ingestion rates, and top-queried databases across every KQL database inside the Eventhouse. Individual KQL databases expose their own narrower, per-database metrics [S1].

*Inference:* This hierarchy maps naturally to organizational roles: platform operations teams watch the container overview for capacity signals, while data engineering teams own per-database metrics for their specific workloads.

### Access Control and Sharing

Sharing an Eventhouse link propagates the sender's permission level across all child items: KQL databases, tables, dashboards, functions, materialized views, and embedded querysets. Sharing an individual KQL database, by contrast, grants access only to that database and excludes Eventhouse-level navigation — the system overview and the database list are not visible [S1].

This distinction is important for security design. Teams that should see only their database should be shared at the database level. Administrators and platform operators who need the full picture should receive the Eventhouse link.

## Anomaly Detection and Native Analytics

Eventhouses include native anomaly detection that evaluates live time-series and event datasets in place, without requiring data copies or exports [S2]. The in-place design reduces detection latency and supports direct investigation from dashboards — engineers can pivot from an anomaly alert to a live KQL query in the same session [S2].

## How It Works and Best Practices

### OneLake Availability Configuration

When enabling OneLake availability, scope the setting intentionally. Database-level enablement is convenient for workloads where all tables are Fabric-shared, but table-level enablement offers more precision — useful when some tables contain sensitive data that should not be exposed to downstream engines without additional controls [S1].

### Cold-Start Latency

An Eventhouse compute node becomes available within 5 to 10 seconds of a cold start, because the engine is fully managed and autoscales [S1]. Architects designing latency-sensitive pipelines that may experience idle periods should account for this warm-up window. For use cases with strict sub-second SLAs, keep the Eventhouse active by ensuring a baseline query or ingestion rate that prevents the engine from going fully idle.

### Surge Protection for Multi-Tenant Platforms

Workspace-level surge protection allows capacity administrators to cap each workspace's share of total CU consumption as a percentage over a rolling 24-hour window. When a workspace breaches its threshold it is automatically blocked from accepting new operations. High-priority workspaces can be designated as mission-critical to exempt them from these rules [S1].

*Inference:* For platform teams hosting multiple business units on shared Fabric capacity, surge protection is the primary instrument for preventing one noisy-neighbor workspace from starving others during peak ingestion events.

## What Goes Wrong

### DDL Operations Blocked While OneLake Availability Is Enabled

Several DDL operations are blocked on a table while OneLake availability is active: renaming the table, changing a column's data type, applying row-level security, and deleting or purging rows [S1]. Attempting these operations without first disabling OneLake availability will fail. Disabling it allows the operation to proceed, but re-enabling it afterward triggers a full historic backfill — which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive on large tables [S1].

**Recommended mitigation:** Complete schema design and row-level security configuration before enabling OneLake availability. Treat the enable step as a milestone, not a toggle to flip back and forth.

### Throttling Under Capacity Pressure

When query demand exceeds available capacity, an Eventhouse applies throttling in three escalating stages [S1]:

1. **Proactive** — queries are slowed but ingestion continues unaffected.
2. **Reactive** — both queries and ingestion are paused, though no data is lost during the pause.
3. **Extreme-reactive** — ingestion and queries are paused with a risk of data loss after a holding period.

The extreme-reactive stage is the critical one: prolonged capacity exhaustion can result in event loss. Workloads with zero-loss ingestion requirements must monitor CU utilization proactively and configure surge protection or scale-up policies before reaching this stage [S1].

### Small-File Accumulation in OneLake

The adaptive batching mechanism that writes KQL data to OneLake delays writes until enough data accumulates to produce optimally-sized Parquet files — typically 200 to 256 MB per file [S1]. The default maximum delay is up to 3 hours. That delay can be reduced to as little as 5 minutes via the mirroring policy, but doing so risks producing many small files that degrade downstream query performance for consumers such as Spark and Power BI Direct Lake [S1].

**Rule of thumb:** Leave the mirroring latency at its default (up to 3 hours) unless you have a specific downstream consumer that requires fresher OneLake data and can tolerate the file-size trade-off.

## Performance and Internals

### UpTime: The Billing Unit

Capacity consumption for an Eventhouse is metered through an **UpTime** metric. The CU seconds consumed equal the number of active seconds multiplied by the virtual core count that the autoscaler has allocated to that Eventhouse at that moment. When a KQL database is a child item of an Eventhouse — the standard configuration — its UpTime rolls up to the Eventhouse item. No separate CU line appears for the database sub-item [S1].

This rollup means you cannot attribute CU cost to individual KQL databases directly from the capacity metrics — you see the Eventhouse's total. *Inference:* Teams that need per-database cost attribution should use per-database monitoring metrics and estimate proportional shares, or use separate Eventhouses when chargeback isolation is a hard requirement.

### Two-Tier Storage: Premium Cache and Standard Retention

KQL database storage is split into two independently billed tiers [S1]:

- **Premium cache tier** (comparable to ADLS premium storage): holds the hot dataset governed by the **caching policy**.
- **Standard tier** (comparable to ADLS hot storage): holds the full retention window governed by the **retention policy**.

Configuring a shorter cache window reduces premium-tier spend without reducing the total queryable history — data beyond the cache window is still queryable from the standard tier, albeit with higher latency as it is fetched from slower storage [S1].

This two-tier model gives practitioners a direct cost lever: set the caching policy to match the period your dashboards and alerts actually query in real time (e.g., last 7 days), and let the retention policy cover the full compliance window (e.g., 90 days or 2 years) at lower cost.

### OneLake Write Batching: The Parquet File-Size Mechanic

When OneLake availability is active, an adaptive batching mechanism governs how frequently data is flushed from the KQL engine to OneLake [S1]. Writes are delayed until the engine can assemble Parquet files in the 200–256 MB range. The default maximum delay is up to 3 hours; the configurable minimum is 5 minutes via the mirroring policy [S1].

The mechanism is adaptive: during high-throughput ingestion, files are written more frequently because data accumulates quickly to the target size. During low-throughput periods, the engine waits longer. The practical consequence is that OneLake latency is inversely correlated with ingestion volume — the more data flowing in, the fresher the OneLake copy.

### Three-Stage Throttling Architecture

The throttling system is designed with graduated degradation rather than a hard cutoff [S1]:

| Stage | Effect on Queries | Effect on Ingestion | Data Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proactive | Slowed | None | None |
| Reactive | Paused | Paused | None |
| Extreme-reactive | Paused | Paused | Possible loss after hold |

The proactive stage exists precisely to shed query load before ingestion is affected — preserving the data-capture function even under analytical pressure. The extreme-reactive stage introduces data-loss risk only after a holding period, giving the system time to recover before events are discarded [S1].

## Worked Example: IoT Fleet Telemetry Pipeline

Consider a fleet management team ingesting vehicle telemetry — GPS coordinates, engine metrics, and diagnostic codes — from 50,000 vehicles at roughly 10 events per vehicle per second.

**Setup:**
- One Eventhouse in the Fleet Analytics workspace.
- Three KQL databases inside it: `raw_telemetry`, `aggregated_metrics`, `anomaly_events`.
- OneLake availability enabled at the database level on `aggregated_metrics` for Power BI Direct Lake dashboards [S1].
- OneLake availability enabled at the table level on `anomaly_events` only, to restrict raw engine codes from appearing in downstream Lakehouses [S1].
- Caching policy on `raw_telemetry` set to 3 days (the live operations window); retention policy set to 180 days for regulatory compliance [S1].

**Query patterns:**
- Operations dashboard uses T-SQL endpoint against `aggregated_metrics` for Power BI connectivity without a KQL rewrite [S2].
- Alert system uses native KQL anomaly detection against `raw_telemetry` in-place, triggering on engine temperature deviations without moving data to a separate analytics store [S2].
- Data science team queries `raw_telemetry` via a shortcut from a Lakehouse, accessing it through the `external_table('raw_telemetry_shortcut')` function in KQL [S3].

**Capacity governance:**
- Surge protection set to cap the Fleet Analytics workspace at 40% of total tenant CU over any 24-hour window, leaving headroom for the billing-critical Finance workspace [S1].
- The Fleet Analytics workspace is not marked mission-critical, so it will be blocked when it hits the threshold [S1].

**OneLake flush timing:**
The mirroring policy on `aggregated_metrics` is left at the default (up to 3 hours). At 500,000 events/second the engine hits the 200 MB Parquet threshold well within minutes, so in practice OneLake is updated far more frequently than the maximum delay suggests [S1].

*Inference:* The three-database layout inside a single Eventhouse cleanly separates raw capture, processed aggregates, and alerts without multiplying capacity costs, because all three share the same CU pool. Schema changes on `raw_telemetry` — such as adding a new diagnostic column — can be performed without touching OneLake availability on that database, since availability is only on `aggregated_metrics` and one table in `anomaly_events`.
